item.title: Russian bombing kills 26 people at Ukraine aid centre, Kyiv says
item.description:
To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.
This video can not be playedFigure caption,
Video shows smoke rising from Komyshuvakha blast craterByJaroslav LukivPublished2 November 2026Updated 1 hour ago
At least 26 people were killed after Russian bombs hit an aid distribution centre, in an attack that Ukraine's leader has called "utterly horrific".
Five people were injured and 27 initially reported missing after at least nine 3,000kg aerial bombs hit the village of Komyshuvakha in the southern Zaporizhzhia region, regional head Mykhailo Semikin said.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said that after the first strike on the local school "used for humanitarian needs", there was a second attack on the place where people were sheltering.
He posted a video showing a huge crater left after Monday's attack, and rescuer teams searching through the rubble.
The Russian military has not publicly commented.
Image source, DSNS / ZaporizhzhiaImage caption,
There are fears that the death toll will rise further as a number of people are still under the rubble
Zelensky initially put the death toll at 18, but Ukraine's state emergencies service DSNS later said 24 people, including two rescuers and four police officers, were confirmed to have been killed.
In his video address late on Monday, Zelensky said 26 people were now known to have died.
He earlier said that "the Russians could not have been unaware that the local residents who remained in Komyshuvakha received humanitarian aid there every week" on Monday.
"This is yet another proof that Russia does not want any de-escalation."
He said that after a recent successful joint Russian-Ukrainian operation to evacuate civilians from the Russia-occupied southern city of Oleshky during a temporary ceasefire brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump, "there was a moment when the next steps could show that peace is possible".

item.title: Thousands of European troops to rehearse Ukraine deployment in event of peace
item.description:
Image source, PA MediaImage caption,
A British paratrooper takes part in a previous Nato training exercise less than 50km (31 miles) from the Russian border in FinlandByJonathan Beale Defence correspondentPublished3 hours ago
Britain and France are to lead a military exercise to test a multinational force's ability to deploy to Ukraine, if there is a peace deal.
Nearly 3,000 military personnel from 12 European nations will take part in the rehearsal in neighbouring Poland this month.
Plans for a reassurance force for Ukraine were set out last year as one of the long-term security guarantees being proposed by European nations.
But there are still more questions than answers as to how such a military force might work in practice. Western officials stress that any force sent to Ukraine would not take part in offensive operations or be involved in peacekeeping or ceasefire monitoring missions.
Nor would they be operating under the command of Nato or on the front line.
Officials say their presence would be to provide reassurance to Ukraine and to help rebuild its armed forces.
The US has been involved in discussions, but is not contributing to the mission.
Russia has already voiced opposition to foreign troops being stationed in Ukraine and, last year, President Vladimir Putin said they would be "legitimate targets".
Western officials have declined to spell out the rules of engagement if any international troops were to be attacked in Ukraine. Though they say the force would be able to defend itself.
UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the exercise showed Britain, France and their allies were stepping up preparation for the day when peace came to Ukraine.
He said: "This is not a hypothetical plan, it's a real force, ready to help Ukraine once the fighting stops."
Lt Gen Tom Bateman, the UK commander of the Multi National Force – Ukraine (MNF-U), said the exercise represented an important step in translating political commitments into credibl...

item.title: Plane may have broken apart ahead of deadly Florida jet crash, say investigators
item.description:
To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.
This video can not be playedFigure caption,
Dashcam footage captures Florida private jet crashByNardine SaadPublished1 November 2026Updated 3 hours ago
The US National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) says it will investigate whether parts of a jet that crashed in Florida broke off before it nose-dived and exploded, killing all nine people on board.
The Learjet 60, which was travelling from Austin, Texas to the Bahamas on Sunday, crashed on a street nine miles (14 km) from President Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago resort.
A tech entrepreneur and his young family, as well as the 20-year-old copilot, were among those who died.
The NTSB said on Monday that it would also investigate to what extent ice and turbulence may have been contributing factors.
To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.
This video can not be playedFigure caption,
Final moments before deadly Florida plane crash
It confirmed that, after the jet took off from Austin, the crew transmitted to air traffic control that they were encountering ice and moderate turbulence.
"We are picking up precipitation, requesting to climb to 37,000 feet if able," the crew said.
NTSB member Tom Chapman said that less than 30 seconds later, the plane began to descend and the crew issued a mayday call.
The transmission then became "unintelligible", he said, adding that: "Sadly, all aboard were lost."
The NTSB said that ice and turbulence were factors in the crash but that determining its probable cause will be a "lengthy investigatory process".
Thunderstorms had been reported in the area at the time.
Officials are also trying to find out whether a cockpit voice recorder was on board at the time of the crash and if it can be recovered.

item.title: Shop freezers in seven European countries hit by cyber-attack
item.description:
To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.
This video can not be playedFigure caption,
'All this food is now useless': Piles of rubbish after shop freezers hit by cyber-attackByJames GregoryPublished2 November 2026
Dozens of supermarkets across seven European countries have been hit by a cyber-attack affecting their refrigerators and freezers.
Around 40 Delhaize supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected, while a smaller number of shops were hit in Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.
Sabcobel, a Belgian company that manufactures some of the affected refrigerators, said the units' evaporators were switched to defrost mode, causing them to warm up, in what is believed to be the same method used in last month's incident that hit hundreds of French supermarkets.
Millions of euros worth of food had to be thrown away in October, local media reported at the time.
Image source, TT NEWS AGENCY / AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption,
Freezers have had to be emptied at several ICA grocery stores in Sweden after the cyber-attack
Stephan Moelans, the CEO of Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize's systems, on Monday told the Belga news agency that the incident was a cyber-attack and that the company had been "working all night and morning to disconnect the affected units from the network".
He said since the French attack in early October, the company had been working to "protect our customers fridges against this vulnerability" but that the units needed physical modifications, not just software updates.
Most supermarkets across Europe are linked to the internet, and maintenance and troubleshooting can be done remotely.
"The simplest solution is to manage the fridges over a secure internet connection. Most of our customers switched to that after the attack in France," Moelans added.
The temperature of freezers in several shops across Europe reportedly rose to as high as 50C (122F).

item.title: Fighting returns to Kherson region after longest Ukraine war ceasefire
item.description:
Image source, ReutersImage caption,
Hundreds of Oleshky evacuees arrived back in Ukraine on Saturday after years trapped on the frontlineByLaura Gozzi and Vitaly Shevchenko, Chief analyst, BBC MonitoringPublished2 November 2026
Fighting has resumed in Ukraine's Kherson after a six-day truce brought quiet to the front-line region for the first time in years.
The ceasefire - the longest since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022 - allowed hundreds of people trapped in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky and its surroundings to be evacuated.
On Monday morning, local authorities confirmed that strikes had resumed, saying Moscow had hit a medical facility in Kherson city centre. They also said a 62-year-old woman and a 73-year-old man were injured when a Russian drone attacked the car they were travelling in.
Ukraine also accused Russian forces of using the humanitarian ceasefire to strengthen their military positions, rotate units and deliver ammunition.
"The enemy used the humanitarian pause to set up their positions," said Ukraine's General Staff, adding they had recorded rotation of Russian units, expansion of anti-drone equipment on the roads, and delivery of ammunition.
The Kremlin appeared to corroborate this when spokesman Dmitry Peskov said it was "reasonable to assume that the Ukrainian army also used this period for the necessary regrouping".
"It is a completely standard practice in such situations," he added.
The ceasefire had been brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump. Both Kyiv and Moscow thanked her repeatedly, though no details of her involvement were shared.
An unusual show of cooperation came from Russia's human rights ombudsman Yana Lantratova and her Ukrainian counterpart Dmytro Lubinets. The pair oversaw the ceasefire, travelled into Oleshky and were filmed speaking to residents together. item.title: Legal challenge to Australia's social media ban to start in High Court
item.description:
Image source, Supplied: Digital Freedom ProjectImage caption,
Australian teen Noah Jones is no longer a plaintiff in the case but will attend Tuesday's hearing ByLana LamSydneyPublished2 November 2026
Two days of hearings on a challenge to Australia's landmark social media ban for children will begin at the country's highest court on Tuesday.
In a major test of the world-leading policy, a digital rights group will argue that the ban for under-16s robs children of their right to free communication. A separate challenge launched by platform Reddit will be jointly heard.
Introduced last December, the ban is a key part of sweeping changes the Australian government has spearheaded in recent years on online safety.
Supporters say the ban protects children from harmful content but critics say it is too blunt an instrument and efforts should focus on improving online safety.
The constitutional challenge in Australia's High Court was filed by the Digital Freedom Project a few weeks before the ban started on 10 December last year. The group is lead by New South Wales parliamentarian John Ruddick.
Two teens who originally spearheaded the case, Noah Jones and Macy Neyland, have since withdrawn as plaintiffs though Jones is still expected to attend Tuesday's hearing.
Speaking about the legal challenge last November, Jones told the BBC that there were bad things online but a blanket ban for under-16s was not the right answer.
"We shouldn't be using the resources and money of these social media platforms to try to avoid fines from our government," he said.
"They should be using this money and resources to try to get rid of the predators and harmful content out there."
Reddit also launched a High Court challenge to the ban, arguing the policy has serious implications for privacy and political rights.
The company said it shared Australia's goal of protecting young people online "but there are better and more effective ways" than a ban...

item.title: North Korea denies being behind record $6.3bn Binance hack
item.description:
Image source, ReutersImage caption,
Kim Yo-jong, the sister of North Korea's leader Kim Jong UnByOsmond ChiaBusiness reporterPublished3 November 2026, 00:56 GMTUpdated 1 hour ago
North Korea has denied claims that it was behind the record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack of cryptocurrency exchange Binance, calling the allegations "absurd rhetoric".
Kim Yo-jong, a top Democratic People's Republic of Korea official and the sister of leader Kim Jong Un, said on Tuesday that the accusations are another "sinister attempt" by the US to damage Pyongyang's public image.
The US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), the Secret Service and cyber analysts have said North Korea orchestrated the hack, which has been described as the largest in history.
This is the latest hack to be linked to North Korea, which has been accused of relying on cyber-crime to help finance its sanctioned economy.
Blockchain analysts and the FBI have said the attack was led by state-backed hacking group TraderTraitor.
The FBI has called on industry partners to help block transactions involving cryptocurrency accounts linked to the group.
"The US has made a trite provocation of linking it with the Democratic People's Republic of Korea again," Kim Yo-jong, the director of North Korea's General Affairs Department, said in a statement.
"It is a grave political provocation against the DPRK that the US misleads the international public opinion as if all the cyber crimes in different parts of the world are our deeds," she said.

item.title: Man and boy arrested after allegedly attacking One Nation volunteer with bat
item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption,
The One Nation volunteer remains in a stable condition in hospitalByLana LamSydneyPublished3 November 2026, 01:57 GMTUpdated 4 minutes ago
Two people have been arrested after a volunteer for Australia's right-wing populist party One Nation was allegedly assaulted with a baseball bat.
A man, 37, and a boy, 14, were arrested on Sunday night after an incident outside the volunteer's home in Torquay, about 100km (62 miles) south-west of Melbourne.
The man was charged with assault offences and remanded in custody while the boy was issued with a caution. The volunteer was hospitalised with non-life threatening injuries, police said. He remains in a stable condition.
One Nation's Victorian leader Warren Pickering claimed the attack happened after the pair "interfered with" election signs on the volunteer's property.
Police haven't provided any detail about a motive, but Pickering said the alleged assault was "un-Australian and unacceptable".
"Political violence or intimidation of any kind against anyone is unacceptable in this country," he said.
"If you don't like someone's politics, you vote accordingly. You don't assault them."
On Tuesday, One Nation leader Pauline Hanson visited the injured volunteer at University Hospital Geelong where he is recovering, praising his "resilience" and "belief" in her party.
"He wants to go right back out there and put the signs up," she said outside the hospital.
The party has said the man has serious injuries, and shared a photo of him with severe swelling and bruising to his face.
Victorian Premier Ben Carroll described the attack as "shocking".
"Whether you're wearing a red, a blue, an orange, or a green T-shirt, they are volunteers," he said.
"They are out there doing what they believe is right, and no one should be coming under attack."

item.title: Man guilty of stealing cash from farm owned by South African president
item.description:
Image source, Leon Sadiki/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesImage caption,
Cyril Ramphosa, South Africa's president, has denied any wrongdoingByEd HabershonBBC News, JohannesburgPublished7 hours ago
A court in South Africa has found a man guilty of stealing more than $500,000 (£372,822) in cash from a farm owned by South African president Cyril Ramaphosa, in a case that mired the head of state in an impeachment saga.
Imanuwela David was found guilty of theft on Monday, as well as conspiracy to commit housebreaking with intent to steal at Phala Phala farm in the Limpopo province in 2020.
Froliana Joseph, a cleaner at the property, was also found guilty of conspiracy to commit housebreaking with intent to steal.
Her brother, Ndilinasho Joseph, was acquitted on all charges.
David was accused of breaking into the cattle farm in February 2020 and taking $580,000 (£432,000) in cash from a sofa on the property. David then went on a spending spree, buying a range of cars including three Mercedes - among them one for his girlfriend - a Porsche, two Volkswagens as well as diamond-encrusted Rolex watches and a house.
David told the court he had made the money through businesses including diamonds and Bitcoin, claims the court rejected. The court also found that David was the only one of the two convicted who had any of the stolen cash in his bank account.
Pre-sentencing will take place on 13 November.
There have been many twists and turns in what is known as the Farmgate scandal.
The theft was largely unknown until 2022 when it was brought to light by Arthur Fraser, South Africa's former intelligence chief and an ally for the former president Jacob Zuma, when he claimed that Ramaphosa hid the theft from the police and tax authorities.
Ramaphosa admitted the theft took place but denied any wrongdoing.
An independent panel that same year found Ramaphosa could have questions to answer over the burglary. MPs voted against establishing an impeachment inquiry.

item.title: Dutch police offer record €2m reward in hunt for drug lord
item.description:
Image source, Netherlands policeImage caption,
Dutch police say Jos Leijdekkers is a "key player" in the international cocaine tradeByAlba MorgadePublished2 November 2026
Dutch authorities have offered a record award of €2m (£1.7m/$2.24m) for information leading to the arrest of Jos Leijdekkers, one of Europe's most-wanted men.
The 35-year-old, who is also known as Bolle Jos (Chubby Jos), was previously accused of being "one of the key players in international cocaine trafficking" by Dutch police.
Commenting on the decision to increase the reward ten-fold, Dutch justice minister David van Weel said it was "necessary given the threat that Leijdekkers poses to national security, our democratic rule of law, and the international legal order".
Dutch prosecutors said capturing Leijdekkers was their "highest priority" and any information shared would be kept secret.
Image source, ReutersImage caption,
He was pictured at a church service in Tihun, Sierra Leone, in January 2025
He is listed by Europol, the EU's law enforcement agency, as among their most-wanted fugitives.
In January 2025, Dutch police said he was believed to be living in Sierra Leone and going by the name Omar Sherrif.
Images apparently showing Leijdekkers in the company of President Julius Maada Bio and other officials have previously emerged.
Dutch prosecutors have demanded his extradition but Sierra Leone has refused to cooperate, prompting the EU to cut some aid to the country.
West Africa is a major transit point for cocaine trafficking from Latin America.
In 2024, a court in Rotterdam sentenced Leijdekkers in absentia to 24 years in prison after finding him guilty of smuggling ⁠more than seven metric tons of cocaine.
Several other police investigations in the Netherlands are ongoing.
Leijdekkers has also been sentenced to 79 years in prison in Belgium.
